newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA REVAMPING NATIONAL PAYMENTS SYSTEM.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA REVAMPING NATIONAL PAYMENTS SYSTEM.

text.p: South Africa's national payments system is currently being revamped in a bid to reduce systemic risk and bring it up to par with international standards.
The new system will ultimately link the Reserve Bank to end-users such as retail and stockbroking clients through payment and settlement networks.
The Reserve Bank will be linked to commercial banks through a settlement network which will include payment clearing houses.
This settlement network will in turn be linked to payment networks which will connect commercial banks to customer payment-service providers such as retailers and stockbrokers.

Johann Bence, payment systems specialist at the Reserve Bank said that while South Africa already had an efficient payments system in place, there was a need to review risk reduction issues because of the increasing values moving through the system.

"The Reserve Bank wants the systemic risk to be reduced to more acceptable levels," Bence said. "We assume there will always be a form of residual risk in a system, but we would like to see systemic risk reduced in the economy and by the same token at least get on a par with international standards."
He noted that the standard of a country's payment system was being built into models used by some overseas players in their assessment of a country's credit risk.
Bence said the new system would have far-reaching consequences both for members of the public as well as South Africa's financial markets.
"For the man in the street it means more secure payments, more trust in the system, a more efficient way of making payments and a means of linking him up to a broad spectrum of people."
He said it was hoped that on the financial markets the new system would result in the reduction of settlement dates, such as the current two-week settlement period on the gilts market.

"The whole NPS risk reduction focus will also focus more attention on the settlement risk in the financial markets where there is no real synchronisation of transfer of ownership -- in other words payments versus delivery," he said.
Bence said the central bank aimed to implement the settlement system in the first quarter of 1998, while it was unclear at this stage when commercial banks would slot into the network.
